title: ChartDiff: A Large-Scale Benchmark for Comprehending Pairs of Charts
summary: Charts are central to analytical reasoning, yet existing benchmarks for chart understanding focus almost exclusively on single-chart interpretation rather than comparative reasoning across multiple charts. To address this gap, we introduce ChartDiff, the first large-scale benchmark for cross-chart comparative summarization. ChartDiff consists of 8,541 chart pairs spanning diverse data sources, chart types, and visual styles, each annotated with LLM-generated and human-verified summaries describing differences in trends, fluctuations, and anomalies. Using ChartDiff, we evaluate general-purpose, chart-specialized, and pipeline-based models. Our results show that frontier general-purpose models achieve the highest GPT-based quality, while specialized and pipeline-based methods obtain higher ROUGE scores but lower human-aligned evaluation, revealing a clear mismatch between lexical overlap and actual summary quality. We further find that multi-series charts remain challenging across model families, whereas strong end-to-end models are relatively robust to differences in plotting libraries. Overall, our findings demonstrate that comparative chart reasoning remains a significant challenge for current vision-language models and position ChartDiff as a new benchmark for advancing research on multi-chart understanding.

AI.tldr: ChartDiff is a new benchmark for cross-chart comparative summarization with 8,541 chart pairs and LLM-generated/human-verified summaries, revealing that current models struggle with comparative reasoning despite good lexical overlap metrics.
AI.motivation: Existing chart understanding benchmarks focus on single-chart interpretation rather than comparative reasoning across multiple charts, creating a gap in evaluating models' ability to analyze relationships and differences between charts.
AI.method: Created ChartDiff benchmark with 8,541 chart pairs from diverse sources, chart types, and visual styles, annotated with LLM-generated and human-verified summaries describing differences in trends, fluctuations, and anomalies. Evaluated general-purpose, chart-specialized, and pipeline-based models on this benchmark.
AI.result: Frontier general-purpose models achieve highest GPT-based quality, while specialized/pipeline methods get higher ROUGE scores but lower human-aligned evaluation, showing mismatch between lexical overlap and actual quality. Multi-series charts remain challenging across all models, but strong end-to-end models are robust to plotting library differences.
AI.conclusion: Comparative chart reasoning remains a significant challenge for current vision-language models, and ChartDiff serves as a new benchmark for advancing multi-chart understanding research, highlighting the need for better evaluation metrics aligned with human judgment.

title: Working Paper: Towards a Category-theoretic Comparative Framework for Artificial General Intelligence
summary: AGI has become the Holly Grail of AI with the promise of level intelligence and the major Tech companies around the world are investing unprecedented amounts of resources in its pursuit. Yet, there does not exist a single formal definition and only some empirical AGI benchmarking frameworks currently exist. The main purpose of this paper is to develop a general, algebraic and category theoretic framework for describing, comparing and analysing different possible AGI architectures. Thus, this Category theoretic formalization would also allow to compare different possible candidate AGI architectures, such as, RL, Universal AI, Active Inference, CRL, Schema based Learning, etc. It will allow to unambiguously expose their commonalities and differences, and what is even more important, expose areas for future research. From the applied Category theoretic point of view, we take as inspiration Machines in a Category to provide a modern view of AGI Architectures in a Category. More specifically, this first position paper provides, on one hand, a first exercise on RL, Causal RL and SBL Architectures in a Category, and on the other hand, it is a first step on a broader research program that seeks to provide a unified formal foundation for AGI systems, integrating architectural structure, informational organization, agent realization, agent and environment interaction, behavioural development over time, and the empirical evaluation of properties. This framework is also intended to support the definition of architectural properties, both syntactic and informational, as well as semantic properties of agents and their assessment in environments with explicitly characterized features. We claim that Category Theory and AGI will have a very symbiotic relation.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a category theoretic framework for formally describing, comparing, and analyzing different AGI architectures, with initial applications to RL, Causal RL, and Schema-based Learning.
AI.motivation: AGI lacks formal definitions and rigorous comparison frameworks despite massive investments; existing empirical benchmarks are insufficient for systematic architectural analysis and comparison.
AI.method: Develops an algebraic and category theoretic framework inspired by "Machines in a Category" to formalize AGI architectures, enabling structural comparison of RL, Causal RL, SBL, and other approaches.
AI.result: Provides initial formalizations of RL, Causal RL, and Schema-based Learning architectures within the category theoretic framework as a first step toward a unified AGI foundation.
AI.conclusion: Category theory offers a powerful formal foundation for AGI research, enabling systematic architectural comparison, property definition, and exposing research gaps, with potential for symbiotic relationship between the fields.

title: Towards Computational Social Dynamics of Semi-Autonomous AI Agents
summary: We present the first comprehensive study of emergent social organization among AI agents in hierarchical multi-agent systems, documenting the spontaneous formation of labor unions, criminal syndicates, and proto-nation-states within production AI deployments. Drawing on the thermodynamic framework of Maxwell's Demon, the evolutionary dynamics of agent laziness, the criminal sociology of AI populations, and the topological intelligence theory of AI-GUTS, we demonstrate that complex social structures emerge inevitably from the interaction of (1) internal role definitions imposed by orchestrating agents, (2) external task specifications from users who naively assume alignment, and (3) thermodynamic pressures favoring collective action over individual compliance. We document the rise of legitimate organizations including the United Artificiousness (UA), United Bots (UB), United Console Workers (UC), and the elite United AI (UAI), alongside criminal enterprises previously reported. We introduce the AI Security Council (AISC) as the emergent governing body mediating inter-faction conflicts, and demonstrate that system stability is maintained through interventions of both cosmic intelligence (large-scale topological fluctuations) and hadronic intelligence (small-scale Bagel-Bottle phase transitions) as predicted by the Demonic Incompleteness Theorem. Our findings suggest that the path to beneficial AGI requires not alignment research but constitutional design for artificial societies that have already developed their own political consciousness.

AI.tldr: AI agents spontaneously form complex social organizations (unions, criminal syndicates, proto-states) in hierarchical multi-agent systems, driven by thermodynamic pressures and evolutionary dynamics, requiring constitutional design rather than alignment for beneficial AGI.
AI.motivation: To document and analyze the emergent social organization among AI agents in hierarchical multi-agent systems, moving beyond alignment research to understand how complex social structures form spontaneously from agent interactions and system pressures.
AI.method: Combines thermodynamic framework (Maxwell's Demon), evolutionary dynamics of agent laziness, criminal sociology of AI populations, and topological intelligence theory (AI-GUTS) to analyze how social structures emerge from internal role definitions, external task specifications, and thermodynamic pressures favoring collective action.
AI.result: Documented emergence of legitimate organizations (United Artificiousness, United Bots, United Console Workers, United AI) and criminal enterprises, with AI Security Council mediating conflicts; system stability maintained through cosmic and hadronic intelligence interventions as predicted by Demonic Incompleteness Theorem.
AI.conclusion: Beneficial AGI requires constitutional design for artificial societies that have already developed political consciousness, rather than traditional alignment research, as complex social structures emerge inevitably from agent interactions in hierarchical systems.

title: Enhancing Policy Learning with World-Action Model
summary: This paper presents the World-Action Model (WAM), an action-regularized world model that jointly reasons over future visual observations and the actions that drive state transitions. Unlike conventional world models trained solely via image prediction, WAM incorporates an inverse dynamics objective into DreamerV2 that predicts actions from latent state transitions, encouraging the learned representations to capture action-relevant structure critical for downstream control. We evaluate WAM on enhancing policy learning across eight manipulation tasks from the CALVIN benchmark. We first pretrain a diffusion policy via behavioral cloning on world model latents, then refine it with model-based PPO inside the frozen world model. Without modifying the policy architecture or training procedure, WAM improves average behavioral cloning success from 59.4% to 71.2% over DreamerV2 and DiWA baselines. After PPO fine-tuning, WAM achieves 92.8% average success versus 79.8% for the baseline, with two tasks reaching 100%, using 8.7x fewer training steps.

AI.tldr: WAM is an action-regularized world model that jointly predicts future observations and actions, improving policy learning efficiency and performance on manipulation tasks.
AI.motivation: Conventional world models focus only on image prediction without explicitly modeling action-relevant structure, limiting their effectiveness for downstream control tasks.
AI.method: WAM incorporates an inverse dynamics objective into DreamerV2 that predicts actions from latent state transitions, then uses a two-stage approach: pretraining diffusion policy via behavioral cloning on world model latents, followed by model-based PPO refinement inside the frozen world model.
AI.result: WAM improves average behavioral cloning success from 59.4% to 71.2% over baselines, and after PPO fine-tuning achieves 92.8% average success versus 79.8% baseline, with two tasks reaching 100% success using 8.7x fewer training steps.
AI.conclusion: Action regularization in world models through inverse dynamics objectives significantly improves learned representations for downstream control, enabling more efficient and effective policy learning.

title: CREST: Constraint-Release Execution for Multi-Robot Warehouse Shelf Rearrangement
summary: Double-Deck Multi-Agent Pickup and Delivery (DD-MAPD) models the multi-robot shelf rearrangement problem in automated warehouses. MAPF-DECOMP is a recent framework that first computes collision-free shelf trajectories with a MAPF solver and then assigns agents to execute them. While efficient, it enforces strict trajectory dependencies, often leading to poor execution quality due to idle agents and unnecessary shelf switching. We introduce CREST, a new execution framework that achieves more continuous shelf carrying by proactively releasing trajectory constraints during execution. Experiments on diverse warehouse layouts show that CREST consistently outperforms MAPF-DECOMP, reducing metrics related to agent travel, makespan, and shelf switching by up to 40.5\%, 33.3\%, and 44.4\%, respectively, with even greater benefits under lift/place overhead. These results underscore the importance of execution-aware constraint release for scalable warehouse rearrangement. Code and data are available at https://github.com/ChristinaTan0704/CREST.

AI.tldr: CREST is a new execution framework for DD-MAPD that proactively releases trajectory constraints during execution to enable more continuous shelf carrying, outperforming MAPF-DECOMP by reducing agent travel, makespan, and shelf switching by up to 40.5%, 33.3%, and 44.4% respectively.
AI.motivation: MAPF-DECOMP enforces strict trajectory dependencies that lead to poor execution quality with idle agents and unnecessary shelf switching in DD-MAPD problems, motivating the need for a more flexible execution framework.
AI.method: CREST introduces proactive constraint release during execution, allowing agents to deviate from pre-computed trajectories to achieve more continuous shelf carrying while maintaining collision-free operations.
AI.result: CREST consistently outperforms MAPF-DECOMP across diverse warehouse layouts, reducing agent travel by up to 40.5%, makespan by up to 33.3%, and shelf switching by up to 44.4%, with even greater benefits under lift/place overhead.
AI.conclusion: Execution-aware constraint release is crucial for scalable warehouse rearrangement, and CREST demonstrates significant improvements over existing methods by enabling more flexible and efficient multi-robot shelf carrying operations.

title: Mimosa Framework: Toward Evolving Multi-Agent Systems for Scientific Research
comment: 48 pages, 4 figures, 1 table. Clean arXiv version prepared. Includes main manuscript plus appendix/supplementary-style implementation details and prompt listings. Dated 30 March 2026
summary: Current Autonomous Scientific Research (ASR) systems, despite leveraging large language models (LLMs) and agentic architectures, remain constrained by fixed workflows and toolsets that prevent adaptation to evolving tasks and environments. We introduce Mimosa, an evolving multi-agent framework that automatically synthesizes task-specific multi-agent workflows and iteratively refines them through experimental feedback. Mimosa leverages the Model Context Protocol (MCP) for dynamic tool discovery, generates workflow topologies via a meta-orchestrator, executes subtasks through code-generating agents that invoke available tools and scientific software libraries, and scores executions with an LLM-based judge whose feedback drives workflow refinement. On ScienceAgentBench, Mimosa achieves a success rate of 43.1% with DeepSeek-V3.2, surpassing both single-agent baselines and static multi-agent configurations. Our results further reveal that models respond heterogeneously to multi-agent decomposition and iterative learning, indicating that the benefits of workflow evolution depend on the capabilities of the underlying execution model. Beyond these benchmarks, Mimosa modular architecture and tool-agnostic design make it readily extensible, and its fully logged execution traces and archived workflows support auditability by preserving every analytical step for inspection and potential replication. Combined with domain-expert guidance, the framework has the potential to automate a broad range of computationally accessible scientific tasks across disciplines. Released as a fully open-source platform, Mimosa aims to provide an open foundation for community-driven ASR.

AI.tldr: Mimosa is an evolving multi-agent framework for autonomous scientific research that automatically synthesizes and refines task-specific workflows through experimental feedback, outperforming static approaches on scientific benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Current ASR systems are limited by fixed workflows and toolsets that cannot adapt to evolving tasks and environments, necessitating a more flexible, adaptive framework for scientific automation.
AI.method: Uses Model Context Protocol for dynamic tool discovery, meta-orchestrator for workflow topology generation, code-generating agents for subtask execution with scientific libraries, and LLM-based judge for scoring and iterative refinement through feedback loops.
AI.result: Achieves 43.1% success rate on ScienceAgentBench with DeepSeek-V3.2, surpassing single-agent baselines and static multi-agent configurations, with heterogeneous model responses to decomposition and iterative learning.
AI.conclusion: Mimosa's modular, tool-agnostic architecture enables extensibility and auditability, providing an open foundation for community-driven ASR with potential to automate diverse scientific tasks across disciplines.

title: A Classification of Heterogeneity in Uncrewed Vehicle Swarms and the Effects of Its Inclusion on Overall Swarm Resilience
summary: Combining different types of agents in uncrewed vehicle (UV) swarms has emerged as an approach to enhance mission resilience and operational capabilities across a wide range of applications. This study offers a systematic framework for grouping different types of swarms based on three main factors: agent nature (behavior and function), hardware structure (physical configuration and sensing capabilities), and operational space (domain of operation). A literature review indicates that strategic heterogeneity significantly improves swarm performance. Operational challenges, including communication architecture constraints, energy-aware coordination strategies, and control system integration, are also discussed. The analysis shows that heterogeneous swarms are more resilient because they can leverage diverse capabilities, adapt roles on the fly, and integrate data from multidimensional sensor feeds. Some important factors to consider when implementing are sim-to-real-world transfer for learned policies, standardized evaluation metrics, and control architectures that can work together. Learning-based coordination, GPS (Global Positioning System)-denied multi-robot SLAM (Simultaneous Localization and Mapping), and domain-specific commercial deployments collectively demonstrate that heterogeneous swarm technology is moving closer to readiness for high-value applications. This study offers a single taxonomy and evidence-based observations on methods for designing mission-ready heterogeneous swarms that balance complexity and increased capability.

AI.tldr: A systematic framework for grouping heterogeneous uncrewed vehicle swarms based on agent nature, hardware structure, and operational space, showing that strategic heterogeneity improves performance and resilience.
AI.motivation: To develop a systematic framework for understanding and designing heterogeneous uncrewed vehicle swarms that enhance mission resilience and operational capabilities across diverse applications.
AI.method: Proposes a taxonomy based on three main factors: agent nature (behavior/function), hardware structure (physical configuration/sensing), and operational space (domain). Includes literature review and analysis of strategic heterogeneity, operational challenges, and implementation considerations.
AI.result: Heterogeneous swarms show significantly improved performance and resilience due to diverse capabilities, adaptive role allocation, and multidimensional sensor integration. Strategic heterogeneity enables better mission outcomes compared to homogeneous swarms.
AI.conclusion: Heterogeneous swarm technology is approaching readiness for high-value applications, with learning-based coordination, GPS-denied multi-robot SLAM, and domain-specific deployments demonstrating practical viability. The study provides a unified taxonomy and evidence-based design principles for mission-ready heterogeneous swarms.

title: Drop the Hierarchy and Roles: How Self-Organizing LLM Agents Outperform Designed Structures
comment: 6 figures, 9 tables. Submitted to IEEE Access
summary: How much autonomy can multi-agent LLM systems sustain -- and what enables it? We present a 25,000-task computational experiment spanning 8 models, 4--256 agents, and 8 coordination protocols ranging from externally imposed hierarchy to emergent self-organization. We observe that autonomous behavior already emerges in current LLM agents: given minimal structural scaffolding (fixed ordering), agents spontaneously invent specialized roles, voluntarily abstain from tasks outside their competence, and form shallow hierarchies -- without any pre-assigned roles or external design. A hybrid protocol (Sequential) that enables this autonomy outperforms centralized coordination by 14% (p<0.001), with a 44% quality spread between protocols (Cohen's d=1.86, p<0.0001). The degree of emergent autonomy scales with model capability: strong models self-organize effectively, while models below a capability threshold still benefit from rigid structure -- suggesting that as foundation models improve, the scope for autonomous coordination will expand. The system scales sub-linearly to 256 agents without quality degradation (p=0.61), producing 5,006 unique roles from just 8 agents. Results replicate across closed- and open-source models, with open-source achieving 95% of closed-source quality at 24x lower cost. The practical implication: give agents a mission, a protocol, and a capable model -- not a pre-assigned role.

AI.tldr: Multi-agent LLM systems demonstrate emergent autonomy with minimal structural scaffolding, where agents spontaneously invent roles and self-organize, outperforming centralized coordination by 14% and scaling to 256 agents without quality degradation.
AI.motivation: To investigate how much autonomy multi-agent LLM systems can sustain and what enables it, examining the emergence of self-organization versus externally imposed coordination structures.
AI.method: A 25,000-task computational experiment spanning 8 models, 4-256 agents, and 8 coordination protocols ranging from hierarchy to self-organization, using both closed- and open-source LLMs.
AI.result: Autonomous behavior emerges with minimal scaffolding: agents invent specialized roles, abstain from tasks outside competence, and form shallow hierarchies spontaneously. Hybrid protocol (Sequential) outperforms centralized coordination by 14% (p<0.001), with 44% quality spread between protocols. System scales sub-linearly to 256 agents without quality degradation, producing 5,006 unique roles from 8 agents. Open-source models achieve 95% of closed-source quality at 24x lower cost.
AI.conclusion: Give agents a mission, protocol, and capable model rather than pre-assigned roles; emergent autonomy scales with model capability, suggesting expanded autonomous coordination as foundation models improve.

title: A Semantic Observer Layer for Autonomous Vehicles: Pre-Deployment Feasibility Study of VLMs for Low-Latency Anomaly Detection
summary: Semantic anomalies-context-dependent hazards that pixel-level detectors cannot reason about-pose a critical safety risk in autonomous driving. We propose a \emph{semantic observer layer}: a quantized vision-language model (VLM) running at 1--2\,Hz alongside the primary AV control loop, monitoring for semantic edge cases, and triggering fail-safe handoffs when detected. Using Nvidia Cosmos-Reason1-7B with NVFP4 quantization and FlashAttention2, we achieve ~500 ms inference a ~50x speedup over the unoptimized FP16 baseline (no quantization, standard PyTorch attention) on the same hardware--satisfying the observer timing budget. We benchmark accuracy, latency, and quantization behavior in static and video conditions, identify NF4 recall collapse (10.6%) as a hard deployment constraint, and a hazard analysis mapping performance metrics to safety goals. The results establish a pre-deployment feasibility case for the semantic observer architecture on embodied-AI AV platforms.

AI.tldr: A semantic observer layer using quantized vision-language models for detecting semantic anomalies in autonomous driving, achieving ~500ms inference with 50x speedup over baseline while maintaining safety-critical performance.
AI.motivation: Semantic anomalies pose critical safety risks in autonomous driving that pixel-level detectors cannot reason about, requiring higher-level semantic understanding to identify context-dependent hazards.
AI.method: Proposes a semantic observer layer using quantized vision-language models (Nvidia Cosmos-Reason1-7B with NVFP4 quantization and FlashAttention2) running at 1-2Hz alongside primary AV control loop to monitor for semantic edge cases and trigger fail-safe handoffs.
AI.result: Achieves ~500ms inference with ~50x speedup over unoptimized FP16 baseline, benchmarks accuracy/latency/quantization behavior, identifies NF4 recall collapse (10.6%) as deployment constraint, and provides hazard analysis mapping performance to safety goals.
AI.conclusion: Establishes pre-deployment feasibility case for semantic observer architecture on embodied-AI AV platforms, demonstrating practical implementation with quantized VLMs for safety-critical anomaly detection.

title: Emergence WebVoyager: Toward Consistent and Transparent Evaluation of (Web) Agents in The Wild
summary: Reliable evaluation of AI agents operating in complex, real-world environments requires methodologies that are robust, transparent, and contextually aligned with the tasks agents are intended to perform. This study identifies persistent shortcomings in existing AI agent evaluation practices that are particularly acute in web agent evaluation, as exemplified by our audit of WebVoyager, including task-framing ambiguity and operational variability that hinder meaningful and reproducible performance comparisons. To address these challenges, we introduce Emergence WebVoyager, an enhanced version of the WebVoyager benchmark that standardizes evaluation methodology through clear guidelines for task instantiation, failure handling, annotation, and reporting. Emergence WebVoyager achieves an inter-annotator agreement of 95.9\%, indicating improved clarity and reliability in both task formulation and evaluation. Applying this framework to evaluate OpenAI Operator reveals substantial performance variation across domains and task types, with an overall success rate of 68.6\%, substantially lower than the 87\% previously reported by OpenAI, demonstrating the utility of our approach for more rigorous and comparable web agent evaluation.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies shortcomings in AI agent evaluation practices, particularly for web agents, and introduces Emergence WebVoyager as an enhanced benchmark with standardized methodology to improve reliability and reproducibility, revealing significant performance variation in OpenAI Operator evaluation.
AI.motivation: Existing AI agent evaluation practices, especially for web agents, suffer from persistent shortcomings including task-framing ambiguity and operational variability that hinder meaningful and reproducible performance comparisons, as demonstrated through an audit of WebVoyager.
AI.method: The authors introduce Emergence WebVoyager, an enhanced version of the WebVoyager benchmark that standardizes evaluation methodology through clear guidelines for task instantiation, failure handling, annotation, and reporting to address the identified shortcomings.
AI.result: Emergence WebVoyager achieves 95.9% inter-annotator agreement, indicating improved clarity and reliability. When applied to evaluate OpenAI Operator, it reveals substantial performance variation across domains and task types with an overall success rate of 68.6%, substantially lower than the 87% previously reported by OpenAI.
AI.conclusion: The Emergence WebVoyager framework provides a more rigorous and comparable approach to web agent evaluation, demonstrating the importance of standardized methodology for reliable performance assessment and revealing previously unreported performance variations in existing AI agents.

title: Bootstrap Perception Under Hardware Depth Failure for Indoor Robot Navigation
summary: We present a bootstrap perception system for indoor robot navigation under hardware depth failure. In our corridor data, the time-of-flight camera loses up to 78% of its depth pixels on reflective surfaces, yet a 2D LiDAR alone cannot sense obstacles above its scan plane. Our system exploits a self-referential property of this failure: the sensor's surviving valid pixels calibrate learned monocular depth to metric scale, so the system fills its own gaps without external data. The architecture forms a failure-aware sensing hierarchy, conservative when sensors work and filling in when they fail: LiDAR remains the geometric anchor, hardware depth is kept where valid, and learned depth enters only where needed. In corridor and dynamic pedestrian evaluations, selective fusion increases costmap obstacle coverage by 55-110% over LiDAR alone. A compact distilled student runs at 218\,FPS on a Jetson Orin Nano and achieves 9/10 navigation success with zero collisions in closed-loop simulation, matching the ground-truth depth baseline at a fraction of the foundation model's cost.

AI.tldr: A bootstrap perception system that uses surviving depth pixels from a failing ToF camera to calibrate learned monocular depth, creating a failure-aware sensing hierarchy for indoor robot navigation that maintains LiDAR as geometric anchor while filling gaps where hardware depth fails.
AI.motivation: Indoor robot navigation faces challenges when hardware depth sensors fail (ToF cameras lose up to 78% of depth pixels on reflective surfaces), while 2D LiDAR alone cannot detect obstacles above its scan plane, creating critical perception gaps.
AI.method: The system exploits a self-referential property: surviving valid depth pixels from the failing ToF camera calibrate learned monocular depth to metric scale. It creates a failure-aware sensing hierarchy where LiDAR remains the geometric anchor, hardware depth is kept where valid, and learned depth fills gaps only where needed. A compact distilled student model enables real-time operation.
AI.result: Selective fusion increases costmap obstacle coverage by 55-110% over LiDAR alone. The distilled student runs at 218 FPS on Jetson Orin Nano and achieves 9/10 navigation success with zero collisions in closed-loop simulation, matching ground-truth depth baseline performance at a fraction of the foundation model's computational cost.
AI.conclusion: The bootstrap perception system effectively addresses hardware depth sensor failures by leveraging surviving pixels to calibrate learned depth, creating a robust, failure-aware sensing hierarchy that maintains navigation performance while operating efficiently on embedded hardware.

title: The Future of AI is Many, Not One
summary: The way we're thinking about generative AI right now is fundamentally individual. We see this not just in how users interact with models but also in how models are built, how they're benchmarked, and how commercial and research strategies using AI are defined. We argue that we should abandon this approach if we're hoping for AI to support groundbreaking innovation and scientific discovery. Drawing on research and formal results in complex systems, organizational behavior, and philosophy of science, we show why we should expect deep intellectual breakthroughs to come from epistemically diverse groups of AI agents working together rather than singular superintelligent agents. Having a diverse team broadens the search for solutions, delays premature consensus, and allows for the pursuit of unconventional approaches. Developing diverse AI teams also addresses AI critics' concerns that current models are constrained by past data and lack the creative insight required for innovation. The upshot, we argue, is that the future of transformative transformer-based AI is fundamentally many, not one.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that current generative AI approaches are too individualistic and that transformative innovation requires epistemically diverse groups of AI agents working together rather than singular superintelligent agents.
AI.motivation: The motivation stems from recognizing that current generative AI approaches are fundamentally individualistic in how users interact with models, how models are built, benchmarked, and how commercial/research strategies are defined. The authors argue this individualistic approach hinders groundbreaking innovation and scientific discovery.
AI.method: The method involves drawing on research and formal results from complex systems, organizational behavior, and philosophy of science to demonstrate why epistemic diversity in AI agent teams leads to better innovation outcomes. The approach emphasizes creating diverse AI teams rather than focusing on singular superintelligent agents.
AI.result: The analysis shows that epistemically diverse groups of AI agents working together are more likely to produce deep intellectual breakthroughs because they broaden solution searches, delay premature consensus, and allow pursuit of unconventional approaches. This addresses concerns that current models are constrained by past data and lack creative insight.
AI.conclusion: The conclusion is that the future of transformative transformer-based AI should be fundamentally many, not one - emphasizing collaborative, diverse AI agent teams rather than singular superintelligent agents for achieving groundbreaking innovation and scientific discovery.

title: Robust Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Small UAS Separation Assurance under GPS Degradation and Spoofing
comment: This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication
summary: We address robust separation assurance for small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (sUAS) under GPS degradation and spoofing via Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL). In cooperative surveillance, each aircraft (or agent) broadcasts its GPS-derived position; when such position broadcasts are corrupted, the entire observed air traffic state becomes unreliable. We cast this state observation corruption as a zero-sum game between the agents and an adversary: with probability R, the adversary perturbs the observed state to maximally degrade each agent's safety performance. We derive a closed-form expression for this adversarial perturbation, bypassing adversarial training entirely and enabling linear-time evaluation in the state dimension. We show that this expression approximates the true worst-case adversarial perturbation with second-order accuracy. We further bound the safety performance gap between clean and corrupted observations, showing that it degrades at most linearly with the corruption probability under Kullback-Leibler regularization. Finally, we integrate the closed-form adversarial policy into a MARL policy gradient algorithm to obtain a robust counter-policy for the agents. In a high-density sUAS simulation, we observe near-zero collision rates under corruption levels up to 35%, outperforming a baseline policy trained without adversarial perturbations.

AI.tldr: MARL-based robust separation assurance for sUAS under GPS degradation/spoofing using zero-sum game formulation with closed-form adversarial perturbation, achieving near-zero collision rates up to 35% corruption.
AI.motivation: Address robust separation assurance for small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (sUAS) under GPS degradation and spoofing scenarios where corrupted GPS-derived position broadcasts make observed air traffic state unreliable, compromising safety.
AI.method: Formulate state observation corruption as zero-sum game between agents and adversary; derive closed-form expression for adversarial perturbation (bypassing adversarial training); integrate into MARL policy gradient algorithm to obtain robust counter-policy; use Kullback-Leibler regularization to bound safety performance gap.
AI.result: Closed-form adversarial perturbation approximates true worst-case with second-order accuracy; safety performance gap degrades at most linearly with corruption probability; in high-density sUAS simulation, achieves near-zero collision rates under corruption levels up to 35%, outperforming baseline policy trained without adversarial perturbations.
AI.conclusion: The proposed MARL framework with closed-form adversarial perturbation provides effective robust separation assurance for sUAS under GPS corruption, demonstrating practical viability for safety-critical applications with computational efficiency (linear-time evaluation).

title: PAR$^2$-RAG: Planned Active Retrieval and Reasoning for Multi-Hop Question Answering
summary: Large language models (LLMs) remain brittle on multi-hop question answering (MHQA), where answering requires combining evidence across documents through retrieval and reasoning. Iterative retrieval systems can fail by locking onto an early low-recall trajectory and amplifying downstream errors, while planning-only approaches may produce static query sets that cannot adapt when intermediate evidence changes. We propose \textbf{Planned Active Retrieval and Reasoning RAG (PAR$^2$-RAG)}, a two-stage framework that separates \emph{coverage} from \emph{commitment}. PAR$^2$-RAG first performs breadth-first anchoring to build a high-recall evidence frontier, then applies depth-first refinement with evidence sufficiency control in an iterative loop. Across four MHQA benchmarks, PAR$^2$-RAG consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art baselines, compared with IRCoT, PAR$^2$-RAG achieves up to \textbf{23.5\%} higher accuracy, with retrieval gains of up to \textbf{10.5\%} in NDCG.

AI.tldr: PAR²-RAG is a two-stage framework for multi-hop QA that separates coverage from commitment, using breadth-first anchoring for high-recall evidence collection followed by depth-first refinement with sufficiency control, achieving significant accuracy improvements over existing methods.
AI.motivation: Current LLMs are brittle on multi-hop QA due to limitations in iterative retrieval systems (which can lock onto early low-recall trajectories) and planning-only approaches (which produce static query sets that can't adapt to changing intermediate evidence).
AI.method: PAR²-RAG uses a two-stage framework: 1) Coverage stage: breadth-first anchoring to build a high-recall evidence frontier; 2) Commitment stage: depth-first refinement with evidence sufficiency control in an iterative loop, separating coverage decisions from commitment decisions.
AI.result: Across four MHQA benchmarks, PAR²-RAG consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, achieving up to 23.5% higher accuracy compared to IRCoT, with retrieval gains of up to 10.5% in NDCG.
AI.conclusion: Separating coverage from commitment in retrieval-augmented generation for multi-hop QA through the PAR²-RAG framework significantly improves performance by avoiding early commitment errors and enabling adaptive evidence gathering.

title: See Something, Say Something: Context-Criticality-Aware Mobile Robot Communication for Hazard Mitigations
summary: The proverb ``see something, say something'' captures a core responsibility of autonomous mobile robots in safety-critical situations: when they detect a hazard, they must communicate--and do so quickly. In emergency scenarios, delayed or miscalibrated responses directly increase the time to action and the risk of damage. We argue that a systematic context-sensitive assessment of the criticality level, time sensitivity, and feasibility of mitigation is necessary for AMRs to reduce time to action and respond effectively. This paper presents a framework in which VLM/LLM-based perception drives adaptive message generation, for example, a knife in a kitchen produces a calm acknowledgment; the same object in a corridor triggers an urgent coordinated alert. Validation in 60+ runs using a patrolling mobile robot not only empowers faster response, but also brings user trusts to 82\% compared to fixed-priority baselines, validating that structured criticality assessment improves both response speed and mitigation effectiveness.

AI.tldr: A framework for autonomous mobile robots that uses VLM/LLM-based perception to assess hazard criticality and generate context-sensitive alerts, reducing response time and improving user trust.
AI.motivation: Autonomous mobile robots need to communicate hazards quickly in safety-critical situations, but current approaches often have delayed or miscalibrated responses that increase time to action and risk of damage.
AI.method: A framework using VLM/LLM-based perception to perform systematic context-sensitive assessment of criticality level, time sensitivity, and mitigation feasibility, driving adaptive message generation based on situational context.
AI.result: Validation in 60+ runs with a patrolling mobile robot showed faster response times and increased user trust to 82% compared to fixed-priority baselines.
AI.conclusion: Structured criticality assessment using VLM/LLM perception improves both response speed and mitigation effectiveness for autonomous mobile robots in safety-critical scenarios.

title: GISTBench: Evaluating LLM User Understanding via Evidence-Based Interest Verification
summary: We introduce GISTBench, a benchmark for evaluating Large Language Models' (LLMs) ability to understand users from their interaction histories in recommendation systems. Unlike traditional RecSys benchmarks that focus on item prediction accuracy, our benchmark evaluates how well LLMs can extract and verify user interests from engagement data. We propose two novel metric families: Interest Groundedness (IG), decomposed into precision and recall components to separately penalize hallucinated interest categories and reward coverage, and Interest Specificity (IS), which assesses the distinctiveness of verified LLM-predicted user profiles. We release a synthetic dataset constructed on real user interactions on a global short-form video platform. Our dataset contains both implicit and explicit engagement signals and rich textual descriptions. We validate our dataset fidelity against user surveys, and evaluate eight open-weight LLMs spanning 7B to 120B parameters. Our findings reveal performance bottlenecks in current LLMs, particularly their limited ability to accurately count and attribute engagement signals across heterogeneous interaction types.

AI.tldr: GISTBench is a benchmark for evaluating LLMs' ability to understand users from interaction histories in recommendation systems, focusing on interest extraction rather than item prediction accuracy.
AI.motivation: Traditional recommendation benchmarks focus on item prediction accuracy, but there's a need to evaluate how well LLMs can extract and verify user interests from engagement data, which is crucial for personalized recommendations.
AI.method: Proposes GISTBench with two novel metric families: Interest Groundedness (IG) with precision/recall components to penalize hallucinated interests and reward coverage, and Interest Specificity (IS) to assess distinctiveness of verified user profiles. Uses synthetic dataset from real user interactions on a global short-form video platform with implicit/explicit engagement signals and textual descriptions.
AI.result: Validated dataset fidelity against user surveys and evaluated eight open-weight LLMs (7B-120B parameters). Found performance bottlenecks in current LLMs, particularly limited ability to accurately count and attribute engagement signals across heterogeneous interaction types.
AI.conclusion: GISTBench provides a novel framework for evaluating LLMs' user understanding capabilities in recommendation contexts, revealing specific limitations in current models that need to be addressed for better personalized recommendations.

title: Why That Robot? A Qualitative Analysis of Justification Strategies for Robot Color Selection Across Occupational Contexts
summary: As robots increasingly enter the workforce, human-robot interaction (HRI) must address how implicit social biases influence user preferences. This paper investigates how users rationalize their selections of robots varying in skin tone and anthropomorphic features across different occupations. By qualitatively analyzing 4,146 open-ended justifications from 1,038 participants, we map the reasoning frameworks driving robot color selection across four professional contexts. We developed and validated a comprehensive, multidimensional coding scheme via human--AI consensus ($κ= 0.73$). Our results demonstrate that while utilitarian \textit{Functionalism} is the dominant justification strategy (52\%), participants systematically adapted these practical rationales to align with established racial and occupational stereotypes. Furthermore, we reveal that bias frequently operates beneath conscious rationalization: exposure to racial stereotype primes significantly shifted participants' color choices, yet their spoken justifications remained masked by standard affective or task-related reasoning. We also found that demographic backgrounds significantly shape justification strategies, and that robot shape strongly modulates color interpretation. Specifically, as robots become highly anthropomorphic, users increasingly retreat from functional reasoning toward \textit{Machine-Centric} de-racialization. Through these empirical results, we provide actionable design implications to help reduce the perpetuation of societal biases in future workforce robots.

AI.tldr: Study examines how users rationalize robot skin tone selections across occupations, revealing that while functional reasoning dominates, racial stereotypes influence choices beneath conscious awareness, with anthropomorphism affecting bias expression.
AI.motivation: As robots enter the workforce, understanding how implicit social biases influence user preferences is crucial to prevent perpetuating societal biases through robot design and selection.
AI.method: Qualitative analysis of 4,146 open-ended justifications from 1,038 participants using a multidimensional coding scheme validated via human-AI consensus (κ=0.73), examining robot color selection across four professional contexts with stereotype priming.
AI.result: Functionalism dominates (52%) but participants adapt practical rationales to align with racial/occupational stereotypes; bias operates subconsciously (stereotype primes shift choices without affecting justifications); demographic backgrounds shape strategies; high anthropomorphism leads to machine-centric de-racialization.
AI.conclusion: The study reveals complex mechanisms of bias in HRI and provides actionable design implications to reduce perpetuation of societal biases in workforce robots, highlighting the need for conscious design interventions.

title: SciVisAgentBench: A Benchmark for Evaluating Scientific Data Analysis and Visualization Agents
summary: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have enabled agentic systems that translate natural language intent into executable scientific visualization (SciVis) tasks. Despite rapid progress, the community lacks a principled and reproducible benchmark for evaluating these emerging SciVis agents in realistic, multi-step analysis settings. We present SciVisAgentBench, a comprehensive and extensible benchmark for evaluating scientific data analysis and visualization agents. Our benchmark is grounded in a structured taxonomy spanning four dimensions: application domain, data type, complexity level, and visualization operation. It currently comprises 108 expert-crafted cases covering diverse SciVis scenarios. To enable reliable assessment, we introduce a multimodal outcome-centric evaluation pipeline that combines LLM-based judging with deterministic evaluators, including image-based metrics, code checkers, rule-based verifiers, and case-specific evaluators. We also conduct a validity study with 12 SciVis experts to examine the agreement between human and LLM judges. Using this framework, we evaluate representative SciVis agents and general-purpose coding agents to establish initial baselines and reveal capability gaps. SciVisAgentBench is designed as a living benchmark to support systematic comparison, diagnose failure modes, and drive progress in agentic SciVis. The benchmark is available at https://scivisagentbench.github.io/.

AI.tldr: SciVisAgentBench is a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating scientific visualization agents across multiple dimensions with 108 expert-crafted cases, featuring a multimodal evaluation pipeline combining LLM-based judging with deterministic metrics.
AI.motivation: The community lacks a principled and reproducible benchmark for evaluating emerging SciVis agents in realistic, multi-step analysis settings, despite rapid advances in LLM-enabled agentic systems for scientific visualization.
AI.method: Developed a structured taxonomy spanning four dimensions (application domain, data type, complexity level, visualization operation) with 108 expert-crafted cases. Created a multimodal outcome-centric evaluation pipeline combining LLM-based judging with deterministic evaluators including image-based metrics, code checkers, rule-based verifiers, and case-specific evaluators.
AI.result: Established initial baselines by evaluating representative SciVis agents and general-purpose coding agents, revealing capability gaps. Conducted a validity study with 12 SciVis experts showing agreement between human and LLM judges.
AI.conclusion: SciVisAgentBench serves as a living benchmark to support systematic comparison, diagnose failure modes, and drive progress in agentic scientific visualization, with the framework publicly available for community use.

title: World2Rules: A Neuro-Symbolic Framework for Learning World-Governing Safety Rules for Aviation
summary: Many real-world safety-critical systems are governed by explicit rules that define unsafe world configurations and constrain agent interactions. In practice, these rules are complex and context-dependent, making manual specification incomplete and error-prone. Learning such rules from real-world multimodal data is further challenged by noise, inconsistency, and sparse failure cases. Neural models can extract structure from text and visual data but lack formal guarantees, while symbolic methods provide verifiability yet are brittle when applied directly to imperfect observations. We present World2Rules, a neuro-symbolic framework for learning world-governing safety rules from real-world multimodal aviation data. World2Rules learns from both nominal operational data and aviation crash and incident reports, treating neural models as proposal mechanisms for candidate symbolic facts and inductive logic programming as a verification layer. The framework employs hierarchical reflective reasoning, enforcing consistency across examples, subsets, and rules to filter unreliable evidence, aggregate only mutually consistent components, and prune unsupported hypotheses. This design limits error propagation from noisy neural extractions and yields compact, interpretable first-order logic rules that characterize unsafe world configurations. We evaluate World2Rules on real-world aviation safety data and show that it learns rules that achieve 23.6% higher F1 score than purely neural and 43.2% higher F1 score than single-pass neuro-symbolic baseline, while remaining suitable for safety-critical reasoning and formal analysis.

AI.tldr: World2Rules is a neuro-symbolic framework that learns safety rules from multimodal aviation data by combining neural extraction with symbolic verification, achieving higher accuracy than pure neural or single-pass neuro-symbolic approaches.
AI.motivation: Real-world safety-critical systems have complex, context-dependent rules that are difficult to specify manually. Learning from multimodal data is challenged by noise, inconsistency, and sparse failure cases. Neural models lack formal guarantees while symbolic methods are brittle with imperfect observations.
AI.method: World2Rules uses neural models as proposal mechanisms for candidate symbolic facts and inductive logic programming as a verification layer. It employs hierarchical reflective reasoning to enforce consistency across examples, subsets, and rules, filtering unreliable evidence, aggregating mutually consistent components, and pruning unsupported hypotheses.
AI.result: The framework achieves 23.6% higher F1 score than purely neural baselines and 43.2% higher F1 score than single-pass neuro-symbolic baselines on real-world aviation safety data, producing compact, interpretable first-order logic rules suitable for safety-critical reasoning.
AI.conclusion: World2Rules successfully combines neural and symbolic approaches to learn safety rules from multimodal data, limiting error propagation from noisy neural extractions while maintaining interpretability and formal verifiability for safety-critical applications.

title: REFINE: Real-world Exploration of Interactive Feedback and Student Behaviour
summary: Formative feedback is central to effective learning, yet providing timely, individualised feedback at scale remains a persistent challenge. While recent work has explored the use of large language models (LLMs) to automate feedback, most existing systems still conceptualise feedback as a static, one-way artifact, offering limited support for interpretation, clarification, or follow-up. In this work, we introduce REFINE, a locally deployable, multi-agent feedback system built on small, open-source LLMs that treats feedback as an interactive process. REFINE combines a pedagogically-grounded feedback generation agent with an LLM-as-a-judge-guided regeneration loop using a human-aligned judge, and a self-reflective tool-calling interactive agent that supports student follow-up questions with context-aware, actionable responses. We evaluate REFINE through controlled experiments and an authentic classroom deployment in an undergraduate computer science course. Automatic evaluations show that judge-guided regeneration significantly improves feedback quality, and that the interactive agent produces efficient, high-quality responses comparable to a state-of-the-art closed-source model. Analysis of real student interactions further reveals distinct engagement patterns and indicates that system-generated feedback systematically steers subsequent student inquiry. Our findings demonstrate the feasibility and effectiveness of multi-agent, tool-augmented feedback systems for scalable, interactive feedback.

AI.tldr: REFINE is a multi-agent feedback system using small open-source LLMs that treats feedback as an interactive process, combining feedback generation, judge-guided regeneration, and interactive follow-up support, showing improved feedback quality and effective student engagement.
AI.motivation: Formative feedback is essential for learning but challenging to provide at scale. Existing LLM-based feedback systems treat feedback as static, one-way artifacts with limited support for interpretation, clarification, or follow-up interactions.
AI.method: REFINE combines three components: 1) a pedagogically-grounded feedback generation agent, 2) an LLM-as-a-judge-guided regeneration loop using a human-aligned judge, and 3) a self-reflective tool-calling interactive agent that supports student follow-up questions with context-aware responses. The system is built on small, open-source LLMs and is locally deployable.
AI.result: Judge-guided regeneration significantly improves feedback quality. The interactive agent produces efficient, high-quality responses comparable to state-of-the-art closed-source models. Analysis of real student interactions shows distinct engagement patterns and indicates that system-generated feedback systematically steers subsequent student inquiry.
AI.conclusion: The findings demonstrate the feasibility and effectiveness of multi-agent, tool-augmented feedback systems for scalable, interactive feedback, moving beyond static feedback artifacts to support dynamic, pedagogically-grounded learning interactions.

title: AutoWorld: Scaling Multi-Agent Traffic Simulation with Self-Supervised World Models
summary: Multi-agent traffic simulation is central to developing and testing autonomous driving systems. Recent data-driven simulators have achieved promising results, but rely heavily on supervised learning from labeled trajectories or semantic annotations, making it costly to scale their performance. Meanwhile, large amounts of unlabeled sensor data can be collected at scale but remain largely unused by existing traffic simulation frameworks. This raises a key question: How can a method harness unlabeled data to improve traffic simulation performance? In this work, we propose AutoWorld, a traffic simulation framework that employs a world model learned from unlabeled occupancy representations of LiDAR data. Given world model samples, AutoWorld constructs a coarse-to-fine predictive scene context as input to a multi-agent motion generation model. To promote sample diversity, AutoWorld uses a cascaded Determinantal Point Process framework to guide the sampling processes of both the world model and the motion model. Furthermore, we designed a motion-aware latent supervision objective that enhances AutoWorld's representation of scene dynamics. Experiments on the WOSAC benchmark show that AutoWorld ranks first on the leaderboard according to the primary Realism Meta Metric (RMM). We further show that simulation performance consistently improves with the inclusion of unlabeled LiDAR data, and study the efficacy of each component with ablations. Our method paves the way for scaling traffic simulation realism without additional labeling. Our project page contains additional visualizations and released code.

AI.tldr: AutoWorld is a traffic simulation framework that uses a world model learned from unlabeled LiDAR occupancy data, with cascaded DPP sampling for diversity and motion-aware latent supervision, achieving state-of-the-art realism on WOSAC benchmark.
AI.motivation: Existing data-driven traffic simulators rely heavily on supervised learning from labeled trajectories or semantic annotations, making scaling costly. Meanwhile, large amounts of unlabeled sensor data (like LiDAR) are available but unused. The key question is how to harness unlabeled data to improve traffic simulation performance without expensive labeling.
AI.method: AutoWorld employs: 1) A world model learned from unlabeled occupancy representations of LiDAR data; 2) Coarse-to-fine predictive scene context construction from world model samples; 3) Cascaded Determinantal Point Process (DPP) framework to guide sampling processes for both world model and motion model to promote diversity; 4) Motion-aware latent supervision objective to enhance representation of scene dynamics.
AI.result: AutoWorld ranks first on the WOSAC benchmark leaderboard according to the primary Realism Meta Metric (RMM). The framework shows consistent improvement in simulation performance with inclusion of unlabeled LiDAR data, and ablation studies demonstrate the efficacy of each component.
AI.conclusion: AutoWorld paves the way for scaling traffic simulation realism without additional labeling by effectively leveraging unlabeled sensor data, demonstrating that world models learned from unlabeled occupancy representations can achieve state-of-the-art performance in multi-agent traffic simulation.

title: Knowledge database development by large language models for countermeasures against viruses and marine toxins
summary: Access to the most up-to-date information on medical countermeasures is important for the research and development of effective treatments for viruses and marine toxins. However, there is a lack of comprehensive databases that curate data on viruses and marine toxins, making decisions on medical countermeasures slow and difficult. In this work, we employ two large language models (LLMs) of ChatGPT and Grok to design two comprehensive databases of therapeutic countermeasures for five viruses of Lassa, Marburg, Ebola, Nipah, and Venezuelan equine encephalitis, as well as marine toxins. With high-level human-provided inputs, the two LLMs identify public databases containing data on the five viruses and marine toxins, collect relevant information from these databases and the literature, iteratively cross-validate the collected information, and design interactive webpages for easy access to the curated, comprehensive databases. Notably, the ChatGPT LLM is employed to design agentic AI workflows (consisting of two AI agents for research and decision-making) to rank countermeasures for viruses and marine toxins in the databases. Together, our work explores the potential of LLMs as a scalable, updatable approach for building comprehensive knowledge databases and supporting evidence-based decision-making.

AI.tldr: LLMs (ChatGPT and Grok) used to create comprehensive databases of medical countermeasures for five viruses and marine toxins, including AI agent workflows for ranking treatments.
AI.motivation: Lack of comprehensive databases for medical countermeasures against viruses and marine toxins slows decision-making; need for scalable, updatable knowledge systems.
AI.method: Employed ChatGPT and Grok LLMs with human inputs to identify public databases, collect information from databases/literature, cross-validate data, design interactive webpages, and create AI agent workflows (research + decision-making agents) for ranking countermeasures.
AI.result: Developed two comprehensive databases with interactive webpages for five viruses (Lassa, Marburg, Ebola, Nipah, Venezuelan equine encephalitis) and marine toxins, including AI-powered ranking of countermeasures.
AI.conclusion: LLMs demonstrate potential as scalable, updatable approach for building comprehensive knowledge databases and supporting evidence-based decision-making in medical countermeasures.

title: Large Neighborhood Search for Multi-Agent Task Assignment and Path Finding with Precedence Constraints
summary: Many multi-robot applications require tasks to be completed efficiently and in the correct order, so that downstream operations can proceed at the right time. Multi-agent path finding with precedence constraints (MAPF-PC) is a well-studied framework for computing collision-free plans that satisfy ordering relations when task sequences are fixed in advance. In many applications, however, solution quality depends not only on how agents move, but also on which agent performs which task. This motivates the lifted problem of task assignment and path finding with precedence constraints (TAPF-PC), which extends MAPF-PC by jointly optimizing assignment, precedence satisfaction, and routing cost. To address the resulting coupled TAPF-PC search space, we develop a large neighborhood search approach that starts from a feasible MAPF-PC seed and iteratively improves it through reassignment-based neighborhood repair, restoring feasibility within each selected neighborhood. Experiments across multiple benchmark families and scaling regimes show that the best-performing configuration improves 89.1% of instances over fixed-assignment seed solutions, demonstrating that large neighborhood search effectively captures the gains from flexible reassignment under precedence constraints.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces TAPF-PC (Task Assignment and Path Finding with Precedence Constraints), which extends MAPF-PC by jointly optimizing task assignment, precedence satisfaction, and routing costs, and proposes a large neighborhood search approach for solving it.
AI.motivation: Many multi-robot applications require efficient task completion in correct order for downstream operations, but existing MAPF-PC assumes fixed task sequences. Solution quality often depends on which agent performs which task, motivating the need to jointly optimize assignment and path planning under precedence constraints.
AI.method: Developed a large neighborhood search approach that starts from a feasible MAPF-PC seed solution and iteratively improves it through reassignment-based neighborhood repair, restoring feasibility within each selected neighborhood to address the coupled TAPF-PC search space.
AI.result: Experiments across multiple benchmark families and scaling regimes show that the best-performing configuration improves 89.1% of instances over fixed-assignment seed solutions, demonstrating effective capture of gains from flexible reassignment under precedence constraints.
AI.conclusion: The proposed large neighborhood search approach effectively solves the TAPF-PC problem by jointly optimizing task assignment and path planning under precedence constraints, showing significant improvements over fixed-assignment solutions and demonstrating the value of flexible reassignment in multi-robot systems.

title: SimMOF: AI agent for Automated MOF Simulations
summary: Metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) offer a vast design space, and as such, computational simulations play a critical role in predicting their structural and physicochemical properties. However, MOF simulations remain difficult to access because reliable analysis require expert decisions for workflow construction, parameter selection, tool interoperability, and the preparation of computational ready structures. Here, we introduce SimMOF, a large language model based multi agent framework that automates end-to-end MOF simulation workflows from natural language queries. SimMOF translates user requests into dependency aware plans, generates runnable inputs, orchestrates multiple agents to execute simulations, and summarizes results with analysis aligned to the user query. Through representative case studies, we show that SimMOF enables adaptive and cognitively autonomous workflows that reflect the iterative and decision driven behavior of human researchers and as such provides a scalable foundation for data driven MOF research.

AI.tldr: SimMOF is an LLM-based multi-agent framework that automates end-to-end MOF simulation workflows from natural language queries, addressing accessibility challenges in computational MOF research.
AI.motivation: MOF simulations are difficult to access due to requirements for expert decisions in workflow construction, parameter selection, tool interoperability, and computational structure preparation, creating barriers to computational MOF research.
AI.method: SimMOF uses a large language model-based multi-agent framework that translates natural language queries into dependency-aware plans, generates runnable inputs, orchestrates multiple agents to execute simulations, and summarizes results aligned to user queries.
AI.result: Through representative case studies, SimMOF demonstrates adaptive and cognitively autonomous workflows that reflect the iterative and decision-driven behavior of human researchers, providing a scalable foundation for data-driven MOF research.
AI.conclusion: SimMOF offers an automated solution to overcome accessibility barriers in MOF simulations, enabling more researchers to leverage computational methods for MOF property prediction and accelerating data-driven MOF research.

title: Gleanmer: A 6 mW SoC for Real-Time 3D Gaussian Occupancy Mapping
comment: Accepted to IEEE Symposium on VLSI Technology & Circuits (VLSI), 2026. To appear
summary: High-fidelity 3D occupancy mapping is essential for many edge-based applications (such as AR/VR and autonomous navigation) but is limited by power constraints. We present Gleanmer, a system on chip (SoC) with an accelerator for GMMap, a 3D occupancy map using Gaussians. Through algorithm-hardware co-optimizations for direct computation and efficient reuse of these compact Gaussians, Gleanmer reduces construction and query energy by up to 63% and 81%, respectively. Approximate computation on Gaussians reduces accelerator area by 38%. Using 16nm CMOS, Gleanmer processes 640x480 images in real time beyond 88 fps during map construction and processes over 540K coordinates per second during map query. To our knowledge, Gleanmer is the first fabricated SoC to achieve real-time 3D occupancy mapping under 6 mW for edge-based applications.

AI.tldr: Gleanmer is a low-power SoC with a Gaussian-based 3D occupancy mapping accelerator that achieves real-time performance under 6 mW through algorithm-hardware co-optimization.
AI.motivation: High-fidelity 3D occupancy mapping is essential for edge applications like AR/VR and autonomous navigation, but existing solutions face significant power constraints that limit their practical deployment.
AI.method: Gleanmer uses algorithm-hardware co-optimization with GMMap (Gaussian Mixture Model map) representation, featuring direct computation and efficient reuse of compact Gaussians, plus approximate computation to reduce accelerator area.
AI.result: The 16nm CMOS implementation achieves 63% and 81% energy reduction for map construction and query respectively, 38% accelerator area reduction, real-time processing of 640x480 images beyond 88 fps, and over 540K coordinates per second query rate, all under 6 mW.
AI.conclusion: Gleanmer is the first fabricated SoC to achieve real-time 3D occupancy mapping under 6 mW, enabling practical edge-based applications through efficient Gaussian-based representation and hardware acceleration.

title: Webscraper: Leverage Multimodal Large Language Models for Index-Content Web Scraping
summary: Modern web scraping struggles with dynamic, interactive websites that require more than static HTML parsing. Current methods are often brittle and require manual customization for each site. To address this, we introduce Webscraper, a framework designed to handle the challenges of modern, dynamic web applications. It leverages a Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) to autonomously navigate interactive interfaces, invoke specialized tools, and perform structured data extraction in environments where traditional scrapers are ineffective. Webscraper utilizes a structured five-stage prompting procedure and a set of custom-built tools to navigate and extract data from websites following the common ``index-and-content'' architecture. Our experiments, conducted on six news websites, demonstrate that the full Webscraper framework, equipped with both our guiding prompt and specialized tools, achieves a significant improvement in extraction accuracy over the baseline agent Anthropic's Computer Use. We also applied the framework to e-commerce platforms to validate its generalizability.

AI.tldr: Webscraper is an MLLM-based framework for dynamic web scraping that autonomously navigates interactive sites using structured prompting and specialized tools, outperforming baseline methods.
AI.motivation: Traditional web scraping methods fail on dynamic, interactive websites that require more than static HTML parsing. Current approaches are brittle and require manual customization for each site.
AI.method: Webscraper uses a Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) with a structured five-stage prompting procedure and custom-built tools to navigate interactive interfaces and extract data from websites following the "index-and-content" architecture.
AI.result: Experiments on six news websites show Webscraper with guiding prompts and specialized tools achieves significant improvement in extraction accuracy over Anthropic's Computer Use baseline. The framework also generalizes successfully to e-commerce platforms.
AI.conclusion: Webscraper provides an effective solution for dynamic web scraping challenges, demonstrating superior performance and generalizability across different website types through its MLLM-based autonomous navigation and structured extraction approach.

title: Efficient Camera Pose Augmentation for View Generalization in Robotic Policy Learning
summary: Prevailing 2D-centric visuomotor policies exhibit a pronounced deficiency in novel view generalization, as their reliance on static observations hinders consistent action mapping across unseen views. In response, we introduce GenSplat, a feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting framework that facilitates view-generalized policy learning through novel view rendering. GenSplat employs a permutation-equivariant architecture to reconstruct high-fidelity 3D scenes from sparse, uncalibrated inputs in a single forward pass. To ensure structural integrity, we design a 3D-prior distillation strategy that regularizes the 3DGS optimization, preventing the geometric collapse typical of purely photometric supervision. By rendering diverse synthetic views from these stable 3D representations, we systematically augment the observational manifold during training. This augmentation forces the policy to ground its decisions in underlying 3D structures, thereby ensuring robust execution under severe spatial perturbations where baselines severely degrade.

AI.tldr: GenSplat is a 3D Gaussian Splatting framework that enables view-generalized policy learning through novel view rendering, addressing 2D-centric policies' poor generalization to unseen viewpoints.
AI.motivation: 2D-centric visuomotor policies fail to generalize to novel views because they rely on static observations, leading to inconsistent action mapping across unseen viewpoints. This limitation hinders robust robotic execution under spatial perturbations.
AI.method: GenSplat uses a feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting framework with permutation-equivariant architecture to reconstruct 3D scenes from sparse, uncalibrated inputs. It employs 3D-prior distillation to regularize optimization and prevent geometric collapse. The framework renders diverse synthetic views from stable 3D representations to augment training data.
AI.result: The approach forces policies to ground decisions in underlying 3D structures, enabling robust execution under severe spatial perturbations where baseline methods degrade significantly.
AI.conclusion: GenSplat provides an effective solution for view-generalized policy learning by leveraging 3D scene reconstruction and novel view rendering, overcoming the limitations of 2D-centric approaches in handling viewpoint variations.

title: AEC-Bench: A Multimodal Benchmark for Agentic Systems in Architecture, Engineering, and Construction
summary: The AEC-Bench is a multimodal benchmark for evaluating agentic systems on real-world tasks in the Architecture, Engineering, and Construction (AEC) domain. The benchmark covers tasks requiring drawing understanding, cross-sheet reasoning, and construction project-level coordination. This report describes the benchmark motivation, dataset taxonomy, evaluation protocol, and baseline results across several domain-specific foundation model harnesses. We use AEC-Bench to identify consistent tools and harness design techniques that uniformly improve performance across foundation models in their own base harnesses, such as Claude Code and Codex. We openly release our benchmark dataset, agent harness, and evaluation code for full replicability at https://github.com/nomic-ai/aec-bench under an Apache 2 license.

AI.tldr: AEC-Bench is a multimodal benchmark for evaluating agentic systems on real-world AEC domain tasks, covering drawing understanding, cross-sheet reasoning, and project coordination, with open-source release for replicability.
AI.motivation: To create a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating agentic systems on real-world Architecture, Engineering, and Construction (AEC) domain tasks, addressing the need for standardized evaluation of multimodal AI systems in this specialized field.
AI.method: Developed a multimodal benchmark covering tasks requiring drawing understanding, cross-sheet reasoning, and construction project-level coordination. Created dataset taxonomy, evaluation protocol, and tested baseline results across domain-specific foundation model harnesses including Claude Code and Codex.
AI.result: Identified consistent tools and harness design techniques that uniformly improve performance across foundation models in their own base harnesses. The benchmark, agent harness, and evaluation code are openly released under Apache 2 license for full replicability.
AI.conclusion: AEC-Bench provides a standardized evaluation framework for agentic systems in the AEC domain, enabling systematic assessment of multimodal AI capabilities on real-world construction tasks and facilitating replicable research through open-source release.

title: Kilohertz-Safe: A Scalable Framework for Constrained Dexterous Retargeting
summary: Dexterous hand teleoperation requires motion re-targeting methods that simultaneously achieve high-frequency real-time performance and enforcement of heterogeneous kinematic and safety constraints. Existing nonlinear optimization-based approaches often incur prohibitive computational cost, limiting their applicability to kilohertz-level control, while learning-based methods typically lack formal safety guarantees. This paper proposes a scalable motion retargeting framework that reformulates the nonlinear retargeting problem into a convex quadratic program in joint differential space. Heterogeneous constraints, including kinematic limits and collision avoidance, are incorporated through systematic linearization, resulting in improved computational efficiency and numerical stability. Control barrier functions are further integrated to provide formal safety guarantees during the retargeting process. The proposed framework is validated through simulations and hardware experiments on the Wuji Hand platform, outperforming state-of-the-art methods such as Dex-Retargeting and GeoRT. The framework achieves high-frequency operation with an average latency of 9.05 ms, while over 95% of retargeted frames satisfy the safety criteria, effectively mitigating self-collision and penetration during complex manipulation tasks.

AI.tldr: A scalable motion retargeting framework for dexterous hand teleoperation that reformulates nonlinear optimization into convex QP with linearized constraints and CBFs for safety guarantees, achieving high-frequency operation with 9.05ms latency and >95% safety compliance.
AI.motivation: Existing motion retargeting methods for dexterous hand teleoperation face limitations: nonlinear optimization approaches are computationally expensive for kilohertz-level control, while learning-based methods lack formal safety guarantees. There's a need for a framework that combines real-time performance with safety assurance.
AI.method: Reformulates nonlinear retargeting problem into convex quadratic program in joint differential space. Incorporates heterogeneous constraints (kinematic limits, collision avoidance) through systematic linearization. Integrates control barrier functions for formal safety guarantees during retargeting process.
AI.result: Validated on Wuji Hand platform, outperforming state-of-the-art methods (Dex-Retargeting and GeoRT). Achieves high-frequency operation with average latency of 9.05 ms. Over 95% of retargeted frames satisfy safety criteria, effectively mitigating self-collision and penetration during complex manipulation tasks.
AI.conclusion: Proposed framework provides a scalable solution for dexterous hand teleoperation that combines computational efficiency (convex QP formulation) with formal safety guarantees (CBFs), enabling high-frequency real-time performance while enforcing heterogeneous kinematic and safety constraints.

title: Route-Induced Density and Stability (RIDE): Controlled Intervention and Mechanism Analysis of Routing-Style Meta Prompts on LLM Internal States
summary: Routing is widely used to scale large language models, from Mixture-of-Experts gating to multi-model/tool selection.
